The Ecology of the Umbrawells
Life Flourishing Below
Although the arachnid is a 
dweller of the Umbrawells, 
it relies on algae-lit waters 
to illuminate the fish that 
swim below for it to catch. 
While it hangs patiently, 
sharp spurs radiate from 
its abdomen to deter other 
predators
Thick stout legs end in 
hooked tarsi that rest 
above the water's surface, 
ready to pull fish into 
their venomed mandibles
Water drips from a stalactite, an acidic tang permeates the air and thousands of crimson glowing spores reflect off the damp stone floor, lighting the way 
for the Traveler to venture deeper in and sate their curiosity on what may grow in these sunless depths. Looking up, the Traveler spies little furred bodies 
among the garden of fungus above, blind bats silently plucking mushrooms into their mouths. 
With pencil in hand, the Traveler sketches in the kaleidoscope of vibrant fungi and little families of mollock. Surprised by just how illuminated the 
abundant life is in these depths —having expected cramped, pitch-black crevices, lifeless and forlorn — the Traveler, instead, found a kind of sickly, alien 
landscape of bacterial mats and fungus, but a beautiful flourishing life nonetheless. Gripping their journal closely, the Traveler breathes in the sulfur-
tinged air and nods to themselves. They are here to learn and explore and, so, deeper they must go.
Through the eons, climate upheavals and devastating mass extinction have nearly scoured life from the surface time and time again. 
With life's tenacious need to survive, many species have slowly wormed their way beneath the earth to survive. Safe from the harsh 
radiation of the sun and erratic changes in climate, beneath tons of stone and dirt, life used other sources of energy. Deep wells of 
sulphuric lakes underneath the earth gave rise to acidophilic microorganisms that have since established the building blocks of a new 
form of biome that thrived in the darkness, the Umbrawells. Like the crushing depths of the ocean, the extremophiles that eke out a 
living in this lightless biome rely on incredibly effective use of the environment's resources, conservation of energy and the guiding 
light of bioluminescence. 
With the fall of the tide, great gaping cavern mouths reveal themselves, burrowing into the south western limestone cliffs of Sol’Kesh. 
Their sunken depths are home to all manner of sea creatures that harbor in the safety of the dark confines. Esslinter in particular make 
great use of the tight tunnels, erupting from crevices in a storm of violence to pull rauka and skith into their abyssal burrows, though 
at times they may find daellash attempting to encroach on the same claustrophobic confines. Deeper into the cliff faces, above the 
waterline, thick mats of silk line the wet tunnels. What may seem, at first, to be a safe and dry escape from the underwater horrors, 
instead offer nothing but the attention of the monstrously enormous, eight-limbed apex predator.
Descending into Peril
For those willing to delve into the Umbrawells, the effort to 
discover the underground dwellers and the riches within are 
seldom worth the fatal risk. Through the acidic foundation that 
has slowly evolved and carved its own unique landscape into these 
depths, new unseen landscapes have taken root. For the lucky few 
that can traverse its endless quiet tunnels and acidic black waters, 
this is a land like no other. Travel deep enough, and one will step 
upon fields of dimly glowing mold-grass under a glittering ceiling 
of silken worms, surrounded by towering fungal growths spewing 
spores that drift down like snow. It's all too easy for one used to the 
sky above, to think they've stepped onto a new planet all together.
With such an unfamiliar landscape revealing new niches for 
animals to grow into, many evolved at a frightening pace to take 
advantage of them first through adaptive radiation: blind fish 
multiplied in sunken, unlit lakes; maddening clicks of thousands 
of echolocating beetles rush through vertical shafts; even sun-
loving lizards have managed to keep warm in the alkaline waters, 
once they developed the durability to withstand the acid.
Travelers that set out to study and reap the nearly alien life of the 
Umbrawells will find that the true danger is not the multitude of 
predatory creatures, but the winding tunnels that worm deeper 
and deeper under the earth. Within a mere hour of travel, any 
sense of direction can be lost as paths twist and cross upon each 
other. Distant tunnels glow with the promising light of the sky 
only to be met with more bioluminescent fungi. And worse still, 
the lure of curiosity, as so few have stepped within these lands: the 
temptation of the next tunnel bend, the glow of a crack in the wall, 
and a chattering call echoing from below. All too easily, a Traveler 
may journey deeper than the point of no return.
